transcript:
Meeting header: Date/Time: 2025-05-07 15:30 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Luca Patel, Jordan Park (Redwood) — Anika Rao, Tomás García, Rachel Lim, Priya Nair (Sycamore Capital)

Summary: (auto) quick notes: Sycamore is evaluating Redwood for low-latency inference for several trading/analytics pipelines. Main compliance constraints: EU/GDPR jurisdictional processing, HIPAA for a small set of healthcare-linked investments, strict log retention and redaction for customer PII, and contractual clause preventing certain outbound egress to non-approved cloud regions. They are leaning toward Dedicated or Private, need auditables.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, I'm Maya from Redwood, and I think we have about 55 minutes together. Luca and Jordan are with me; Luca will cover the private deployment bits.
[00:12] Anika Rao: Thanks Maya. We're mainly scoped on residency and log controls today. We have EU clients and some US healthcare streams, so we'll need both GDPR and HIPAA covered.
[00:19] Tomás García: And procurement's sorta on the call to listen for any vendor blockers, like forming an approved deployment topology.
[00:25] Rachel Lim: Quick callout — our ML infra currently lives in our GCP org, but security wants to avoid sending decrypted PII out of our VPC.
[00:32] Luca Patel: Totally — that's the use case where Private in VPC mode or Dedicated with VPC peering usually fits. We support customer-managed network boundaries and can do private link style connectivity.
[00:41] Priya Nair: From procurement we also need to know if logs or model inputs will ever be stored in Redwood-hosted S3 or similar, because some counterparties forbid third-party storage.
[00:49] Maya Chen: Short answer: hosted will persist things for troubleshooting unless you opt out; Dedicated or Private can be configured to avoid any long-term storage on Redwood side. We'll put the specific SLAs and retention options in the doc.
[00:58] Anika Rao: Can you clarify what "avoid storage" means? Are you talking ephemeral only or zero-copy? We need guarantees for EU residents that data never leaves region X.
[01:10] Jordan Park: For Private we can run the control plane in your VPC or a customer-managed control plane depending on contract; for strict EU residency we typically recommend the Private deployment so compute and state remain in the customer's region.
[01:23] Tomás García: What about key management? We need KMS or HSM integration so Redwood doesn't have access to plaintext keys.
[01:31] Luca Patel: We integrate with customer KMS — Cloud KMS, AWS KMS, and can do HSM-backed keys where the customer controls key rotation. With that flow, logs that contain tokens or decrypted payloads can be redacted client-side.
[01:42] Rachel Lim: Is there an option for client-side encryption of inputs before they hit the model? We've looked at partial homomorphic-type approaches but mainly want to reduce exposure in audit logs.
[01:52] Maya Chen: Client-side encryption for inputs is possible if you pre-process; the runtime expects plaintext for inference so keys need to be accessible to the runtime. For fully opaque ops you'd need an on-prem private runtime. That's why many of our finance customers pick Private.
[02:07] Anika Rao: On GDPR specifically: we need data residency at rest and transit in the EU, plus DSAR support — ability to erase individual records. How does Redwood support that?
[02:19] Luca Patel: For Private, you control storage so you can honor DSARs directly. For Hosted, we have data-deletion APIs and retention controls, but you still have to accept that meta logs might be in Redwood infra unless contractually excluded.
[02:32] Tomás García: How often do you see hosted being acceptable for companies with EU-only customers?
[02:38] Maya Chen: It depends — if you can accept contractual commitments and an EU region that we operate, hosted can work. But if you require legal isolation and auditability (and no provider-level access), Private is recommended.
[02:49] Rachel Lim: Another asks: PCI or financial regs, we need specific audit fields in logs — trade id, user id, model version, input hash, redaction flag. Can Redwood provide those?
[02:59] Jordan Park: Yes, we have an audit logging schema that can be extended. We had to add fields for a finance customer last quarter, so we can surface model_version, request_hash, masked_input_indicator, and the routing decision. We'll need to map the field names to your SIEM.
[03:15] Anika Rao: About retention: we have a policy of min 7 years for certain transaction logs in our jurisdiction, but risk team wants the ability to suppress PII after 30 days. Is it possible to retain audit metadata but purge PII?
[03:28] Luca Patel: Absolutely — we support split retention: keep token/metadata for the retention window, but mask or drop the PII fields after X days. That mapping is configurable in Dedicated/Private. Hosted has more limited options due to multi-tenant infra.
[03:41] Tomás García: Does Redwood's hosted log store live in multiple regions? We have a clause restricting export to non-approved countries — e.g., can't replicate logs to the US if original jurisdiction is EU.
[03:53] Maya Chen: Our hosted offering supports regionally segmented storage, but customers requiring strict contractual guarantees often pick Private so replication policies are fully under their control. We can include a clause for region locking in the contract, but Private is the cleanest from a compliance perspective.
[04:07] Rachel Lim: Any compliance certifications we can review? SOC 2, ISO, HIPAA?
[04:12] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 — we'll share the certs and the control mapping. For HIPAA we have a business associate agreement and can support PHI segmentation in Private deployments. I'll attach the attestation. [link to docs: https://redwood.example/legal/soc2 , https://redwood.example/legal/hipaa-attestation]
[04:30] Anika Rao: On HIPAA — only a small product uses PHI but it's sensitive. We'll need signed BAA and evidence of technical safeguards like transmission encryption and access logging.
[04:39] Jordan Park: We can provide a BAA and show technical docs: TLS in transit, AES-256 at rest by default, and customer-supplied KMS ensures keys can't be unilaterally rotated by Redwood.
[04:51] Priya Nair: Procurement question — if we go Dedicated but not Private, do you still retain the right to access logs for debugging?
[04:58] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we can include contractual terms to restrict Redwood-side access; operationally we have a support workflow that requires customer approval for root cause debugging. In a lot of enterprise contracts we limit support access and require jump boxes in customer VPCs.
[05:10] Tomás García: How does the model rollout policy interact with compliance? If we do canary to a newer model, do old requests remain queryable? We need an immutable ledger of what model served which request for audit.
[05:21] Luca Patel: We record model_version and can pin model versions per-route. All requests have an immutable audit record (metadata) even if payloads are purged after retention. That metadata is what you would use for audits.
[05:33] Rachel Lim: Is there an option to redact or hash request text in logs while still keeping a deterministic identifier? We prefer a hash so we can trace without keeping full text.
[05:41] Jordan Park: Yes, request hashing (SHA256) is common — we store a hash and a redaction flag. For reproducibility you can keep the plaintext within your own storage and reconcile with the hash.
[05:52] Anika Rao: About DSARs again — we may need to map requests to user identities and then delete those entries; hashing complicates deletion. Thoughts?
[06:01] Maya Chen: If you need per-user deletion, best to keep a mapping table in your environment and treat Redwood logs as append-only audit metadata with no PII. For hosted, we'll provide deletion APIs but you should own the primary mapping if DSARs are frequent.
[06:16] Priya Nair: What about vendor attestations — we need evidence of penetration tests, incident history redacted, and SLAs?
[06:24] Maya Chen: We publish a summary of pen tests and can provide a redacted incident history under NDA. SLA terms are in the enterprise contract — uptime and latency SLOs, and we can include indemnities per negotiation.
[06:36] Tomás García: Any restrictions on how long debug logs are available to Redwood? That affects our breach response playbooks.
[06:43] Luca Patel: Debug logs can be configured to be ephemeral. For Private you control retention; for Dedicated we can negotiate a retention policy in the contract, and debug artifacts are only accessible under approved support requests.
[06:56] Rachel Lim: Are there known limitations around model quantization or hardware that affect determinism for audits? We run deterministic scoring for backtests.
[07:06] Jordan Park: Determinism can be impacted by runtime kernels, especially across different GPUs or quantized paths. For audit-sensitive workflows we recommend pinning model binary + runtime version and running in a single hardware class; we document kernel versions in the audit metadata.
[07:23] Anika Rao: Ok, logistics: what do you need from us to scope a Private PoC?
[07:29] Luca Patel: We'll need target dataset sizes, peak qps, allowed regions, and the list of required audit fields. Also your legal template for contract redlines.
[07:37] Maya Chen: We'll also take a list of the specific controls you need mapped to SOC2/HIPAA/ISO, so we can produce a control mapping spreadsheet.
[07:44] Tomás García: For the PoC, can you support a locked-down environment where we supply VMs and you deploy the runtime?
[07:50] Luca Patel: Yes, we can do customer-hosted control plane where Redwood ships the runtime and/or an ops bundle you run in your env. That's the on-prem pattern some of our regulated customers use.
[07:59] Priya Nair: Pricing question briefly — is Private much more expensive than Dedicated?
[08:04] Maya Chen: Typically Private has higher one-time setup and per-month platform licensing, but Dedicated has reserved capacity pricing. We'll give a side-by-side estimate in the next email.
[08:12] Rachel Lim: Any blockers for initial connectivity? We have strict firewall rules.
[08:17] Jordan Park: We'll provide a whitelist IP range and support private endpoint peering; for on-prem you'd do a site-to-site VPN or direct connect.
[08:25] Anika Rao: On the topic of logging restrictions: we must ensure certain fields never leave our environment — can Redwood support a allow-list of log fields?
[08:34] Luca Patel: Yes, we can implement deny-list or allow-list for log field propagation. We'll include that in the architecture doc.
[08:41] Tomás García: Are there customers in finance using Redwood in EU-only mode?
[08:45] Maya Chen: Yes, a couple of asset managers in the EU run private deployments with EU-only controls; we can provide references under NDA.
[08:54] Priya Nair: For contracting, if we request no US egress for backups, is that feasible?
[08:59] Maya Chen: It's feasible in Private — we can set replication policies to stay within EU zones. Hosted would be harder but we can negotiate region lock clauses.
[09:08] Rachel Lim: We also need to confirm whether model artifacts (weights) are considered customer data — and where they live.
[09:15] Jordan Park: Model artifacts are treated as customer-managed when you bring-your-own-model. If using Redwood-hosted public models, the binaries may be cached; you can request local-only caching or private model upload so everything stays in your storage.
[09:29] Anika Rao: Any other security controls — RBAC, SSO?
[09:33] Maya Chen: We support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit trails for admin actions. For Private we can integrate with your IdP via SCIM.
[09:44] Tomás García: Ok let's wrap — sounds like actionables are SOC2/HIPAA docs, private topology, and a proposed PoC scope.
[09:52] Maya Chen: Agreed. We'll send docs and draft SOW. Luca will prepare the topology and Jordan will cover the audit schema.
[10:00] Priya Nair: Can we get a written note about access controls and support access? That's a procurement must-have.
[10:06] Maya Chen: Yep, we'll include a clause that details support access workflows and approval gates.
[10:12] Rachel Lim: Thanks everyone.
[10:14] (call ends)

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts — "V P C" for VPC, "kay vee cache" for KV cache, and proper nouns sometimes misrecognized. Links and artifacts referenced: SOC2/ISO certs (https://redwood.example/legal/soc2), HIPAA attestation (https://redwood.example/legal/hipaa-attestation), example private topology (to be shared).
